Jean Marx also posed with great clarity the problem of “Robert de Boron and Glastonbury” in Nouvelles recherches, pp. 139–152. This is a typical example of the phenomenon we are considering. Perhaps identifying Avalon with Glastonbury served Plantagenet interests, and perhaps it helped suppress King Arthur’s end-times role in favour of official Church teaching. But would that have been enough to change the Imago Terrae—the image of the Earth—to which we refer here, as the faculty through which a new geographical holy place is discovered or perceived? Whether or not this identification concealed the revival of a Celtic Church suppressed by the Roman Church, it did not necessarily end Arthur’s eschatological role. A hadîth widespread in Shiite Islam says that the bodies of prophets and Imams remain in the tomb for only three days before being carried “to Heaven.” The profound theosopher Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî warns those who might try to prove this by opening their graves: they would indeed find the body they sought. Yet the tomb is empty. For it is another body that is said to be carried “to Heaven,” and “this does not mean the sky above our heads.” Even if King Arthur’s and Queen Guinevere’s remains were found in their tombs at Glastonbury, their “body” (their jism mithâlî, imaginal body) is elsewhere, where the perception of Avalon as the Other World places them. ↩

See Op. metaph. III, p. 299, line 13, where the edited text reads something like: “This Grail is what lies buried beneath (what is concealed by) our old woollen cloak.” It is edifying, but hardly original; we ourselves once understood the passage this way. Yet the Istanbul Râghib 1480 manuscript (unfortunately unavailable for the published critical apparatus) has a vigorous, precise scholar’s hand, though regrettably without diacritical dots. In it, the reading of the word elsewhere interpreted as pashmîneh (“woollen”) becomes problematic. A few years ago, our friend Mr Mo’în and I examined this passage and read in it two Arabic words (lohba sa-tomîtoh) drawn from a source familiar to Sohrawardî and inserted into the Persian verse, as Persian syntax permits: “lohba sat’mitoh”-e mâst. The author applies the meaning of these two words to his own condition. Literally: “This buried Grail (that is, hidden treasure) is our ‘burning flame (or burning thirst) that will cause his death.’” Sohrawardî thus means: for me, this ardour or thirst that ultimately kills is the Grail concealed within me, the Grail that I myself am. Or, as we have tried to translate it, this ardour feeds on our death as it consumes our life. That is why the symbol of the Grail meets the symbol of the Phoenix here as a symbol of the religio mentis, the religion of the spirit. ↩
